contract.note: The contract rightly finds no capability scale or doubling rule. Choosing a benchmark would rewrite the claim, and a personal evidential judgment cannot be tested as a fact.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own Substack post.

semantics.note: The antecedent (enthusiasm dwindles and valuations plummet) is kept. The consequent ('won't disappear', 'will still have their place') is firm language, so it is a scorable conditional forecast. His wording is kept.

contract.note: The plain reading is fair and ordinary: both conditions must hold as a sector-wide contraction, and survival means continued practical use. No numeric thresholds are added. No deadline was stated.

evidence.note: Reuters, Oct 2026: market stress, pulled listings and more selective investors, but investment continues. This does not establish a sector-wide valuation collapse with fading enthusiasm.
Kiplinger, Oct 2026: private AI valuations still rising and enthusiasm strong. This cuts against the antecedent having occurred.

reviews.rationale: No dated episode in the packet meets both antecedents. e1 shows some public-market stress, while e2 shows enthusiasm and private valuations still rising. Because the antecedent has not been established, continued LLM use cannot count as the forecast's outcome. The conditional is not scored, and with no deadline it stays open.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words. He is rejecting Mollick's quoted claim; the quote is not his claim, but the rejection is.

semantics.note: The proposition keeps the 'if my graphs are remotely correct' qualifier and the 5-14 month doubling threshold. Dropping Mollick's name does not change the commitment. It is a retrospective observation, not a forecast.

contract.note: The contract rightly finds no defined capability scale. Doubling accuracy, halving errors and compute efficiency are different tests, and picking one would supply the claim's central meaning.

evidence.note: Ho et al. measure the compute needed to reach a fixed performance level, not capability doubling. This is background on Mollick's source, not evidence about the outcome.

reviews.rationale: The claim depends on an undefined 'capabilities doubling' rate and on the rough accuracy of his own graphs. No objective measure or doubling rule exists to test it. The only evidence item shows the 5-14 month figure concerns compute efficiency, which is context only.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own Substack post.

semantics.note: The proposition keeps all four reported developments, the 'recent weeks' window, and the hedges 'largely' and 'serious questions'. It adds no causal claim.

contract.note: The plain reading is fair: a window of March 1 to April 13, 2024; 'largely closed' as substantial dismantling of the original organization, not legal dissolution; 'struggling' as ordinary distress; and the critique needs to exist, not be proved correct.

evidence.note: CMA decision: the vast majority of Inflection staff and the core team moved to Microsoft after the March 19, 2024 deal. This supports 'largely closed shop'.
Inflection's own disclosure: the company continues under a new CEO with an API business. This fits the 'largely' qualifier and does not negate the staff departure.
FT via Ars Technica, April 1, 2024: CEO resignation, restive investors, monthly losses. This supports 'struggling'.
TechCrunch, April 3, 2024: Ghost Autonomy shut down, and it had explored LLMs for driving.
Secondary summary timestamped April 13, 2024 shows the Internet of Bugs Devin critique was circulating before the post. Weak source, but dated.
80 Level, April 16, 2024: identifies the same video as recent and describes its substantive complaints.
Futurism, 2025: names the critic as software engineer Carl Brown and dates the video to April. Corroborates who made the critique.

reviews.rationale: All four items fall within the window. Inflection's core team left for Microsoft on March 19 (e1); continued corporate existence fits 'largely' (e2). Stability was in distress after its CEO resigned (e3). Ghost shut down on April 3 (e4). A software engineer's YouTube critique of Devin was circulating by April 13 (e5-e7).
